items.readable_text:
Content:
Recall that the probability density function (or pdf) of a continuous random variable [MATH: X] defined over a set [MATH: S] is a function [MATH: f(x)] that satisfies the following conditions:

Content:
- [MATH: f(x) \geq 0] for all [MATH: x] in [MATH: S]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1]

Content:
The probability that [MATH: X] lies in the interval [MATH: [a,b]] is given by
[MATH: P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.]

Content:
This probability can be interpreted as the area bounded between [MATH: f(x)] and the [MATH: x]-axis over the interval [MATH: x\in [a,b],] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a9519601d1f8ace1a5ba4ecf75b73e30]

Content:
Also, remember that for continuous random variables, we get the same answer whether or not we include the endpoints of an interval [MATH: [a,b].] In other words,

Content:
[MATH: P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X < b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b).]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll get some practice at computing probabilities with continuous random variables.

sections.normalized_html:
If a continuous random variable [MATH: X] has the probability density function [MATH: f(x),] then [MATH: P(a \lt X \lt b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.]

So, in our case, we have

[MATH: P(1 < X < 3)|= ∫_{1}^{3}f(x)dx; = ∫_{1}^{3}(1)/(18)(x^{2} − 1)dx; = (1)/(18)∫_{1}^{3}(x^{2} − 1)dx; = (1)/(18)[(1)/(3)x^{3} − x]_{1}^{3}; = (1)/(18)([(1)/(3)(3)^{3} − (3)] − [(1)/(3)(1)^{3} − (1)]); = (1)/(18)([9 − 3] − [(1)/(3) − 1]); = (1)/(18)(6 + (2)/(3)); = (1)/(18) ⋅ (20)/(3); = (10)/(27).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Recall that the probability density function (or pdf) of a continuous random variable [MATH: X] defined over a set [MATH: S] is a function [MATH: f(x)] that satisfies the following conditions:

Content:
- [MATH: f(x) \geq 0] for all [MATH: x] in [MATH: S]
- [MATH: \displaystyle \int_{S} f(x) \, \textrm dx = 1]

Content:
The probability that [MATH: X] lies in the interval [MATH: [a,b]] is given by
[MATH: P(a \leq X \leq b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.]

Content:
This probability can be interpreted as the area bounded between [MATH: f(x)] and the [MATH: x]-axis over the interval [MATH: x\in [a,b],] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a9519601d1f8ace1a5ba4ecf75b73e30]

Content:
Also, remember that for continuous random variables, we get the same answer whether or not we include the endpoints of an interval [MATH: [a,b].] In other words,

Content:
[MATH: P(a \leq X \leq b) = P(a < X < b) = P(a < X \leq b) = P(a \leq X < b).]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll get some practice at computing probabilities with continuous random variables.

---

Item 2 — Example: Computing the Probability That a Random Variable Lies Within a Bounded Interval

Example Prompt:
Compute [MATH: P\left( 1 \lt X \lt 3 \right)] given that the random variable [MATH: X] has the probability density function

[MATH: {(1)/(18)(x^{2} − 1),|1 ≤ x ≤ 4,; 0,|otherwise.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
If a continuous random variable [MATH: X] has the probability density function [MATH: f(x),] then
[MATH: P(a \lt X \lt b) = \int_a^b f(x) \, \textrm dx.]

So, in our case, we have

[MATH: P(1 < X < 3)|= ∫_{1}^{3}f(x)dx; = ∫_{1}^{3}(1)/(18)(x^{2} − 1)dx; = (1)/(18)∫_{1}^{3}(x^{2} − 1)dx; = (1)/(18)[(1)/(3)x^{3} − x]_{1}^{3}; = (1)/(18)([(1)/(3)(3)^{3} − (3)] − [(1)/(3)(1)^{3} − (1)]); = (1)/(18)([9 − 3] − [(1)/(3) − 1]); = (1)/(18)(6 + (2)/(3)); = (1)/(18) ⋅ (20)/(3); = (10)/(27).]
